The Treasury was the Federation's advertisement for success. The Midas is the
Federation admitting that, past a certain net worth, the point of a ship is no
longer to go anywhere — it is to be seen having the ship. Every surface a hand
might touch is gold; every surface a hand will never touch is also gold, because
someone, someday, might check. The structural alloy is electrum, chosen over
cheaper metals that would have performed identically. The viewports are cut from
a single block of synthetic diamond, for a clarity no passenger has ever once
remarked upon. There are no weapons — a Midas does not fight; it is escorted,
insured, and, if the worst occurs, replaced. The drive merely sips fuel and the
hull is armored far past any sane requirement, because the one indignity its
owner will not tolerate is failing to arrive. The Federation builds exactly as
many as there are billionaires willing to commission them, and not one more.
It checks.
items.prestige_lock: Locked: prestige hull reserved for pilots who have earned a secret achievement.

items.name: Midlife Crisis
items.description: Outer Rim liner. Frontier luxury for people whose definition of luxury is flexible.
items.lore: The Midlife Crisis is what passes for a luxury liner on the Rim. The viewing lounges have actual windows (reinforced glass, not portholes). The quarters have doors that close (most of the time). The bar serves drinks that are technically beverages (by frontier health standards). It's fast enough to outrun boredom and has enough fuel to reach the interesting parts of the galaxy. Passengers are mostly retired prospectors spending their earnings, adventurers who can't sit still, and the occasional fugitive enjoying the view.

items.name: Mineral Rights
items.description: A Crimson Siege Drill rebuilt from steel and salvage. Two weapons, one mining laser. Goes to other people's claims and leaves with what's in the asteroid.
items.lore:
A Siege Drill rebuilt from steel and salvage. The tungsten frame and titanium plating that let the original absorb return fire are gone — cheaper materials, lighter hull, takes hits harder for it. Two weapon mounts and the mining laser stayed because those are the parts that matter. Pirates call theirs the Mineral Rights because mineral rights, in practice, belong to whoever can enforce them. The ship goes to someone else's claim, establishes what the rights are, and leaves with the ore. The original holders are not, at that point, in a position to dispute the outcome.
'

items.name: Money Pit
items.description: Outer Rim mobile refinery. Processes raw ore in the field. Eats fuel accordingly.
items.lore: The Money Pit earns its name twice: once for the cost to build it, and again for the fuel it consumes running the onboard refinery. Rim miners discovered that processing ore in the field eliminates the round trip to a station, which more than compensates for the Money Pit's voracious appetite. The refinery equipment was reverse-engineered from Nebula Trade Federation designs with what Rim engineers describe as "creative liberties." It runs hot, loud, and slightly off-spec. The refined materials come out fine. Mostly.

items.name: Monopoly
items.description: Nebula trade cruiser. Protects commercial interests with energy drain weapons and economic leverage.
items.lore: The Monopoly-class is the Federation's most feared non-capital warship, not because of its weapons — though those are adequate — but because of its electronic warfare suite. The Monopoly's energy drain systems siphon power from hostile ships, degrading their weapons, shield_operation, and propulsion simultaneously. Engaging a Monopoly is an exercise in diminishing returns: the longer the fight continues, the weaker you get and the stronger it gets. The Federation calls this "hostile acquisition." Pirates call it "the reason we avoid Federation convoys." The four utility slots run market analysis even during combat, because the Federation never stops calculating.

items.name: Morningstar
items.description: Armored Crimson fuel tanker. Supplies the fleet or sells to the desperate at markup.
items.lore: Wars run on fuel, and the Morningstar keeps Crimson fleets moving. The default armor plate drops it to a crawl, but tankers don't need speed — they need to survive the trip. The heaviest hull in the Crimson T2 lineup protects fuel tanks that keep an entire strike group operational. Losing a tanker loses the operation, so the Fleet armors them like warships and assigns escorts that know better than to leave formation. The Morningstar's secondary role as a mobile fuel depot makes it one of the few Crimson ships that turns a profit without firing a shot: stranded pilots in deep space pay whatever the captain asks. Fleet accountants call this "field-expedient pricing."

items.name: Motherlode
items.description: Nebula long-range prospecting miner. Scanner-equipped for deep-field ore surveys.
items.lore: Federation mining operations learned that the real margins aren't in moving more ore — they're in finding the right deposit before anyone else does. The Motherlode ships with an integrated scanner suite and an oversized fuel tank for surveying distant asteroid fields that shorter-range miners never bother reaching. The weapon mount is gone entirely — prospectors don't fight, they file claims. The hold is modest by Nebula standards, but compression storage and a strong yield bonus mean every trip justifies the fuel spent getting there. The best Motherlode pilots know where every unclaimed belt within range sits, and they keep that information closer than their nav coordinates.

items.name: Munitions Foundry
items.description: Crimson mobile weapons factory. Converts raw ore directly into ammunition and weapon components.
items.lore:
The Munitions Foundry-class is the Crimson Fleet's military-industrial
complex condensed into a single hull. Feed it raw ore, and the internal
smelters, forges, and assembly lines produce ammunition, weapon
components, and replacement parts without ever docking at a station.
The Fleet designed it to sustain prolonged campaigns in enemy territory
where supply lines are contested. Two weapon mounts protect the
investment — losing a Munitions Foundry sets fleet operations back
weeks. The foundry systems run hot enough to require dedicated cooling
infrastructure, which explains the tonnage that doesn't go to cargo.

items.name: Muster
items.description: Crimson liner. Moves Fleet families and garrisons between postings.
items.lore:
Garrison rotations move thousands of Fleet families a year, and the Pact
does not entrust its families to civilian contractors. The Muster is
armored like a warship, scheduled like an operation, and decorated like
neither. Boarding begins on the hour. Departure is on the hour. The
seats recline exactly eleven degrees, a figure derived from a study on
transit readiness that no one has been able to locate. Children receive
a window seat and a logistics workbook. Veterans ride free, which is the
only sentimental policy in the Fleet, and the one no quartermaster has
ever proposed cutting.

items.name: Nebula Tender
items.description: Nebula shuttle. Efficient personnel and light cargo transfers.
items.lore:
The Tender-class exists because freighters cost fuel and time costs money.
For station-to-station transfers and light cargo runs, a smaller hull with an
oversized fuel tank delivers better per-unit margins than anything else in the
fleet. Fifty-six jumps on a single tank means fewer refueling stops, fewer
docking fees, and fewer line items on the quarterly report. The passenger cabin
is comfortable enough that VIP transport contracts occasionally cover the
operating cost twice over.

items.name: Nebulae
items.description: Solarian armored gas harvester. Dual collection arrays behind reinforced plating for hazardous operations.
items.lore: The Confederacy designed it for contested gas clouds where lighter harvesters get chased off — heavy hull plating and a default armor package that makes it the hardest industrial ship to kill in its class. The armor drops speed to a crawl, which the engineering committee accepted after calculating the fuel savings: slower ships burn less fuel per jump, stretching the tank far beyond what faster harvesters can manage. Dual gas collection arrays handle throughput while the hull absorbs whatever the neighborhood throws at it. Pilots who want speed can strip the plate, but the Nebulae was built to outlast problems, not outrun them.

items.name: Nebulous
items.description: Voidborn adaptive gas condenser. Massive CPU and open slots let pilots build it however they want.
items.lore: The Nebulous extracts gas through resonant membrane arrays that vibrate at frequencies unique to each cloud's composition — adapting in real time without pilot input. The hull shimmers faintly during extraction, condensation forming patterns that Voidborn engineers photograph but don't explain. With only a harvester and shield booster fitted by default, the remaining fitting capacity dwarfs anything else in the gas harvester class. The shield array regenerates damage faster than most gas clouds can inflict it, which is fortunate — the hull underneath is tissue-thin by T2 standards. The best yield bonus in class comes standard. What pilots do with the rest of the space is their problem.

items.name: Need to Know
items.description: Outer Rim intelligence cruiser. Sees everything, says nothing, moves suspiciously fast.
items.lore:
Speed 3 on a large hull with top-tier sensors and processing power.
The Need to Know-class is the Outer Rim's dedicated intelligence
platform — capable of passive surveillance, signal interception, and
the kind of deep-space reconnaissance that makes other empires nervous.
The Rim officially denies operating intelligence ships. The Need to
Know-class is officially listed as a "long-range survey vessel" in
all public records. Its crew carry credentials identifying them as
"geological researchers." Nobody is fooled, but the paperwork is
technically in order.

items.name: No Appeal
items.description: Commandant Voss's flagship. A Crimson Executioner with the berserker plating swapped for salvage armor and the boarding systems left untouched. Voss built his operation on taking ships intact. The slow speed has never bothered him — he chooses his ground and holds it.
items.lore:
The walls of Voss Redoubt are patched with hull plating from a dozen different ship classes. Every piece came from a ship that tried to leave Alhena space without permission. Commandant Voss has been running the same operation for long enough that the patch history is visible in the architecture.
The No Appeal is the operational expression of Voss's doctrine: it doesn't chase, it doesn't negotiate, and it doesn't leave. The flight deck deploys assault craft while the weapon mounts suppress point defense, and the boarding bays process whatever remains. The fury alloy and crimson siege plating that gave the original its armor rating are gone — the rebuilt hull takes hits harder. Voss considers this appropriate. His crew earns their place. The ship earns its reputation the same way.

items.name: No Exit
items.description: Archon Mera's flagship. A Solarian Interdictor rebuilt without the logic matrix and solar collector array that made the original's gravitational field precisely calibrated. What's left is less precise and draws more power than the engineering crew would prefer. Ships inside the field can still run. They can't jump. On trading lanes, that's generally sufficient.
items.lore:
The Solarian Confederacy spent decades insisting a gravitational interdiction field was theoretically impossible before building one and proving themselves wrong. Archon Mera spent considerably less time on the theoretical side. She wanted the field. She stripped the ship for what she couldn't source and rebuilt from what she could.
The Solarian logic matrix and solar collector arrays are gone — no one in Zaniah space fabricates the mathematics that calibrated the original's interdiction field. The processing cores are salvage. The rebuilt field is less precise, less stable, and draws enough power that the engineering crew has developed opinions about it. Ships inside it can still move. They cannot jump. On trading lanes, where every ship's emergency plan is the same jump sequence, this tends to be decisive.
The Mera Sanctum sits in a sensor shadow. Mera positioned it there deliberately — nothing approaches without her knowing. The No Exit is the second part of the strategy. By the time a target understands what ship they're looking at, the name has already become accurate.

items.name: No Refunds
items.description: Fast Rim fighter. Hits hard, breaks easy, and the name covers the warranty.
items.lore:
The No Refunds is what happens when Rim engineers decide a fighter's
job is to hit something before it hits back. Speed 5 with a missile launcher
and autocannon gives it the second-highest damage output of any T1 fighter,
which is good, because the 110-point hull and minimal shielding mean it
can't afford a long engagement. The standard loadout includes an armor
plate that most pilots quietly appreciate. One free utility hardpoint lets
the owner customize — fuel extender for range, scanner for bounty work,
whatever keeps you flying.

items.name: Nomad
items.description: Outer Rim fleet runner. Fastest carrier in the cluster. Still slow, but fastest.
items.lore: Out on the Rim, waiting for a shuttle back is not a plan. The Nomad-class was built by confederates who kept losing time running empty ships home after a job, and solved it by building a carrier that could keep up — roughly. It is not fast. No carrier is fast. But it is the least slow, which counts for a lot when fuel costs money and pirates have patrol routes. Eight bays, four utility slots for whatever the crew jury-rigged this week, and enough fuel reserve to make a long crossing without stopping. The Nomad does not have a home base. That is the point.

items.name: Noumenon
items.description: Voidborn deep-space explorer. Detects phenomena that shouldn't exist.
items.lore: Voidborn deep-space expeditions routinely report wormholes in systems that other empires surveyed and found empty. The sensor arrays aboard the Noumenon detect spatial distortions that standard instruments filter out as background noise — topology that folds in ways the math says it shouldn't, gravity gradients with no visible source, exit signatures from transits that haven't happened yet. The layered shield envelope keeps the ship intact while the crew investigates the difference between a stable wormhole and whatever the other kind turns out to be. Whether the Noumenon finds wormholes or whether they form in response to observation remains, fittingly, unresolved.

items.name: Observatorium
items.description: Solarian research cruiser. Capital-grade sensor arrays for phenomena other ships cannot detect.
items.lore: The Observatorium-class is the Confederacy's answer to the fundamental question of astrophysics: "What are we not seeing?" Seven utility slots support the most comprehensive sensor architecture ever mounted on a mobile platform. The processing array — the most powerful on any T4 hull — runs predictive models, spectral analysis, and gravitational mapping simultaneously. Nine hundred units of fuel give it the endurance to reach phenomena that shorter-ranged vessels only theorize about. Solarian research councils compete fiercely for Observatorium deployment schedules, as a single expedition typically generates enough data for dozens of doctoral theses.

items.name: Off the Books
items.description: Director Sable's flagship. An Outer Rim fleet command ship rebuilt without the condensed dark matter drives that gave the original its speed. The sensor arrays, coordination suite, and six utility slots are exactly where they were. The Outer Rim built the original so their civilian government could deny what their military was doing. Sable finds this purpose equally applicable, for different governments, for different operations, for the same reasons.
items.lore:
The Outer Rim built the Plausible Deniability to coordinate military operations while giving the civilian government something to deny. The name reflects the ship's secondary function: making whatever just happened look like "unauthorized freelance activity." Director Sable found this framing professionally useful.
The condensed dark matter drives are gone. The titanium alloy is gone. The rebuilt hull is slower and softer. The coordination suite is intact. The sensor arrays are intact. The six utility slots that support every conceivable command function are intact. Sable runs his operation professionally — clear categorization, no loose ends, everything accounted for. The Off the Books is what he calls the category for operations that don't appear in the accounting.
Sable Port runs like a business. It is, by most definitions, a business. The ships that leave it don't file reports. The operations they conduct don't generate paperwork. The Off the Books coordinates all of it, which is why the name is accurate in both directions: the ship doesn't appear in anyone else's records, and neither does anything it commands.

items.name: Oil Money
items.description: Outer Rim whaling ship. Harpoons the cloud-whale pods, renders them in the hold, hauls the oil home — that's the whole business plan.
items.lore: The Oil Money is named for the only thing about it anyone cares about: the cloud-whale pods are out there fat with oil and worth a hull apiece, and this is the cheapest thing on the Rim that can go get them and come back. Not a warship — too precious, and the pods don't shoot back. Not a harvester — no teeth. The Oil Money splits the difference: three harpoon mounts on a slow, deep-range working hull, a hold big enough to flense a whole pod into oil and baleen on the way home, and just enough plate to shrug off a panicking whale's tail. It will never win a fight against anything with guns, and the crews know better than to point it at the big lonely shapes that haunt the deep neon banks — an Oil Money that picks a fight with a full-grown Cloudwhale comes home as salvage, if it comes home. But turn it loose on a pod of pilot-whales and it pays for itself in a single run, try-pots smoking, hold filling, the oldest trade in the galaxy carried out into the dark.

items.name: Omnibus
items.description: Solarian transit bus. Scheduled, punctual, sufficient.
items.lore:
Omnibus: Latin, "for all." The Office of Civic Mobility spent four years
determining the optimal seating arrangement, and the result is fourteen
berths whose comfort rating is "adequate" according to the standards body
the Confederacy established to rate seating. The Omnibus runs its routes
whether or not anyone is aboard, because the schedule is the point. No
one has ever described it as luxurious, including the design committee,
whose final report described it as "sufficient, which was the objective."
Junior researchers, retired couples, visiting lecturers, and everyone's
luggage arrive together, on time, having shared an experience none of
them will mention again.

items.name: Omniscience
items.description: Voidborn research titan. Studies phenomena by becoming part of them.
items.lore:
The Omniscience-class does not study phenomena from a distance. Its
organic sensor arrays extend into the fabric of whatever it is
observing, becoming temporarily entangled with the subject of study.
Research data from an Omniscience contains information that was not
and could not have been measured by the instruments aboard. Solarian
peer reviewers have taken to flagging Voidborn research papers with
the note "results reproducible, methodology incomprehensible."
Nine utility slots support a sensor architecture that other empires
describe as "excessive" and the Collective describes as "barely
adequate."

items.name: Opus Magna
items.description: Solarian dreadnought. The Confederacy's masterwork of balanced naval architecture.
items.lore: The Opus Magna represents the pinnacle of Solarian naval engineering — a vessel designed not merely to fight but to embody the Confederacy's philosophy of measured, documented excellence. Every system is triple- redundant. Every weapon mount has its own dedicated fire control processor. The shield array draws from six independent emitters. The design review took twelve years and produced a technical specification longer than most novels. Solarian admirals consider command of an Opus Magna the highest honor in the fleet — and the thickest required reading list.

items.name: Ordinance
items.description: Crimson mass-production combat hull. Three weapons, no frills, reliable in formation. Built from materials the Fleet actually has on hand.
items.lore: Every CPU cycle accounted for, every fitting slot committed, nothing left over for second-guessing. The Pact builds the Ordinance when supply lines are short and the mission cannot wait — a hull that can be fabricated from materials the Fleet stockpiles regardless of trade conditions, at half the build time of anything else in its class. No utility slots, no redundant systems, no concessions to pilot comfort. Not the ship you want for a prolonged campaign. Exactly the ship you want when you need six of them by morning.

items.name: Overdue
items.description: A Nebula Margin with one utility slot replaced by a weapon mount and its delivery manifest replaced by a target list. It can still dock almost anywhere without attracting attention. The Federation built it to arrive on schedule. Pirates found that 'on schedule' was a relative concept.
items.lore: The Nebula Collective runs the most reliable courier network in inhabited space. Their Margin-class docks at every station, in every empire, without a second glance — exactly what a pirate scout operation needs. The sensor suite has been repurposed from optimizing delivery routes to tracking what target ships are carrying and whether they're worth flagging for a raiding squad. One utility slot was sacrificed for a weapon mount, and even that's been fitted flush to the existing hull geometry. It looks like a Margin. It docks like a Margin. The cargo hold still has room for a full scan kit and a fast exit. Nothing about the exterior has changed, and that's the entire point.

items.name: Overhead
items.description: Nebula patrol craft. The operational cost of keeping trade lanes safe, line-itemed and justified.
items.lore: The Overhead-class is what the Federation builds when it calculates the annual cost of piracy against the annual cost of prevention and decides prevention is cheaper. Two pulse lasers provide credible deterrence, the shields keep the asset intact long enough to resolve most engagements, and the oversized cargo hold is officially designated for "evidence processing and contraband seizure." The accounting department approved the hold capacity without asking what evidence typically looks like. Patrol captains appreciate this. The integrated scanner suite identifies cargo manifests, registration discrepancies, and outstanding trade violations at comfortable range. The name appears on the Federation's annual security budget as a line item, which is exactly where the Federation prefers its law enforcement to live.

items.name: Overlord
items.description: Crimson command dreadnought. Fleet coordination backed by personal firepower that demands respect.
items.lore:
The Overlord is where Crimson Fleet admirals command battle groups.
Unlike other empires' command ships, the Overlord carries enough
personal firepower to be a threat in its own right — four weapon
mounts and sixty points of armor ensure that the flagship doesn't
need an escort to survive contact with the enemy. The coordination
suite manages fleet-wide targeting, formation changes, and fire
concentration from systems hardened against electronic warfare. Five
utility slots accommodate the electronic warfare countermeasures,
sensor packages, and communication arrays that keep a Crimson
battle group operating as a single lethal organism. Commanding an
Overlord is the highest rank in the Fleet's operational hierarchy.

items.name: Overmind
items.description: Voidborn carrier. Launches wings of fighters that share a single distributed consciousness.
items.lore:
The Overmind-class carrier does not command its fighter wings. It thinks
them. Each launched craft operates as an extension of the carrier's
biological neural network, sharing sensory data and tactical intent
across a substrate the Collective has never allowed outside researchers
to examine. Pilots of the fighter wings report feeling "part of
something larger" during operations. After docking, the feeling fades
slowly. Some pilots find they miss it. The Collective considers this
expected and says nothing further.

items.name: Palimpsest
items.description: Voidborn intelligence flagship. Reads the electromagnetic echoes of deleted transmissions.
items.lore:
A palimpsest is a manuscript written over an erased earlier text. The
Palimpsest-class applies this principle to electromagnetic radiation,
reading the ghost impressions of signals that were encrypted, scrambled,
or deliberately destroyed. The sensor arrays detect information that
technically no longer exists. Other empires' intelligence services have
spent considerable resources trying to understand how the Palimpsest
intercepts communications that were never sent in the first place.
The Collective's only public comment: "All information exists. Some
has simply been forgotten."

items.name: Pantheon
items.description: Solarian drone carrier. Fleet-scale autonomous operations with centralized oversight.
items.lore: The Pantheon-class manages a constellation of autonomous drones the way the Confederacy manages a galaxy — with layers of oversight, comprehensive logging, and periodic performance reviews. The quad-core processing array coordinates dozens of independent units while the six utility slots accommodate drone bays, electronic warfare suites, and repair systems. Each drone's mission parameters require committee approval. The approval process has been automated, but the committee still convenes monthly to review the automation's decisions.

items.name: Paradox
items.description: Voidborn light fighter. Shield-dominant defense, unsettling targeting.
items.lore:
Enemy pilots report that the Paradox-class seems to be in two places at
once during combat maneuvers. The shield array regenerates 6 points per tick
with the default recharger installed — faster than most T1 weapons can deplete
it. The targeting system operates on principles that even Collective technicians
describe as "emergent" rather than "designed," producing steady energy damage
while the shields absorb everything incoming. The tradeoff is a hull that wouldn't
survive a hard docking. Sixty points of structure behind two points of armor means
that anything that gets through the shields ends the conversation immediately.

items.name: Paradox Engine
items.description: Solarian interdictor. Area denial through gravitational manipulation.
items.lore: A paradox engine is a thought experiment that shouldn't work but does. The Paradox Engine-class generates gravitational distortions that prevent faster-than-light escape — a feat Solarian physicists spent decades insisting was impossible before grudgingly agreeing to build one anyway. The interdiction field generator draws enormous power, hence the dedicated power core. The theoretical physics department still publishes papers arguing the device shouldn't function. The Navy publishes after-action reports proving it does.

items.name: Parallax
items.description: Voidborn phase scout. Briefly exists in two reference frames simultaneously.
items.lore:
The Parallax is the Collective's first production phase-technology vessel.
Its drive system allows the ship to briefly occupy two positions in
space-time, viewing the same location from two reference frames. The
practical application is reconnaissance that is literally impossible to
intercept — the version of the ship collecting data is not in the same
reference frame as the version that could be detected. Pilots describe
the experience as "looking at yourself from across the room while also
being in the room." The Collective's training manual devotes an entire
chapter to managing the resulting nausea.

items.name: Paramount
items.description: Nebula command cruiser. Coordinates trade convoys and fleet operations.
items.lore:
The Paramount-class serves as the nerve center for Federation trade
convoys and the occasional military operation. The coordination suite
handles route optimization, market analysis, and fleet logistics
simultaneously. Five utility slots support every conceivable support
system, and the generous cargo hold ensures the Paramount generates
revenue even while commanding. Profit and military effectiveness
have always been the same line item on the Federation's balance sheet.

items.name: Partisan
items.description: Crimson elite interceptor. Small, fast, and lethal — a veteran's knife, and only veterans can fly it.
items.lore: Most Crimson hulls are built to be replaced. The Partisan is built to be earned. It is a sliver of a ship — barely more than a cockpit, a reactor, and three weapon mounts strapped to an engine that has no business being that size. There is no armor worth the name and almost no margin for error, and that is by design: the Partisan is flown by pilots who have already proven they do not make errors. In the right hands it is impossible to pin and impossible to ignore, slipping inside a cruiser's guard, opening it up, and gone before the return fire arrives. In the wrong hands it is a brief and expensive smear. The Fleet keeps the piloting requirement deliberately punishing. A Partisan handed to a rookie is a Partisan thrown away, and the Fleet does not throw away the few ships it actually respects.

items.name: Paydirt
items.description: Nebula mega ore hauler. Obscene cargo capacity. Empties asteroid belts and hauls everything to market.
items.lore:
The Paydirt-class exists because the Federation asked "what if we
just... carried more?" Two thousand one hundred sixty cargo capacity is achieved
through structural engineering that other empires consider irresponsible
— the cargo bay occupies over 60% of the hull volume. Zero weapon
mounts because the Federation considers guns on a mining platform a
waste of cargo space. Escorts exist for a reason, and ore in the hold
generates revenue that guns never will. The Paydirt doesn't mine
efficiently — it mines thoroughly, stripping asteroid belts down to
pebbles and hauling everything to market in a single trip.

items.name: Peer Review
items.description: Outer Rim frontier scout. Goes anywhere forever, brings home nothing but data.
items.lore: You build a hull like this when the job is to vanish. One pilot, a fuel reserve that laughs at distance, and instruments sharp enough to read a wormhole's pulse from a system away — that is the whole of it. The Rim crews who fly the Peer Review go out past the last charted gate and stay out, weeks at a stretch, drifting through the deep frontier on a tank that never seems to run dry, logging anomalies nobody back home has names for yet. It hauls almost nothing and it would not survive the first thing that decided to shoot at it, which is exactly why it is fast and why it carries no guns to slow it down. It does not bring back cargo. It brings back the map. The crews who come home say the silence out there is the part you never get used to.

items.name: Pennon
items.description: Crimson officer transport. Gets the commander there at speed.
items.lore:
A pennon is the flag at the tip of a lance. Fleet doctrine holds that
commanders belong with their formations, and when a commander must be
somewhere else, doctrine requires the absence to be brief. The Pennon
exists to keep it brief. Two staterooms forward for the flag party, two
berths aft for the aides, one autocannon in case anyone mistakes a staff
transport for a soft target. The staterooms are spartan by civilian
standards and scandalous by Crimson ones — there are cushions. Junior
officers assigned to escort duty call it the softest posting in the
Fleet, though never in writing.

items.name: Penumbra
items.description: Voidborn electronic warfare frigate. Operates in the space between detection and certainty.
items.lore:
The Penumbra occupies the twilight between visibility and invisibility,
between signal and noise. Its electronic warfare suite doesn't jam enemy
sensors so much as make them question their own readings. Fleet commanders
report that engagements involving a Penumbra have a dreamlike quality —
targets appear where they shouldn't, distances seem uncertain, and time
itself becomes slightly unreliable. The Collective considers this "working
as intended."

items.name: Perigee
items.description: Solarian expedition vessel. Extended-range deep space exploration platform.
items.lore: More fitting capacity than any other exploration vessel in production. The Perigee is less a ship than a configurable scientific platform — anomaly detectors, survey arrays, gravimetric analyzers, whatever the mission profile demands. Solarian expedition protocol requires comprehensive data collection before any transit attempt: map the anomaly, model its terminus, predict its stability. Other empires jump through wormholes and hope. Solarian crews publish their predictions first, then verify them. Crews customize their Perigees so aggressively that no two ships in the fleet share a loadout.

items.name: Perihelion
items.description: Solarian research vessel. Mobile laboratory with comprehensive analysis suites.
items.lore: Every cubic meter aboard the Perihelion serves double duty as laboratory space. The fitting capacity accommodates research instruments that would strain smaller vessels — xenobiology sample containment, spectrographic arrays, gravitational anomaly mapping rigs — and the processing power to analyze everything in the field rather than hauling raw data home. Expedition-grade fuel reserves keep the ship operational deep in uncharted space. Published more peer-reviewed papers per ship-year than any other vessel class in service, which the crews attribute to equipment and the equipment manufacturers attribute to luck.

items.name: Permafrost
items.description: Crimson deep-range ice harvester. Fast, long-legged, built to reach ice fields Crimson space doesn't have.
items.lore: Crimson space is rich in ore and poor in ice. The Shattered Comet Graves at Krynn produce the weakest ice yields in settled space, and waiting for Nebula supply contracts was never strategically acceptable. The Permafrost solves this with speed — a default afterburner pushes it to the fastest industrial hull in Crimson service, built to reach ice fields in neutral space and strip them before anyone organizes a response. Pull the afterburner and the fuel tank stretches to real range, turning the ship into a long-haul ice runner instead. The hold is small either way, so the Fleet runs Permafrost sorties in rotation. One weapon mount keeps claim disputes brief.

items.name: Phase Collector
items.description: Voidborn phase-shift gas harvester. Best extraction rate in class — collects what others can't detect.
items.lore: The collection membranes extend partially into adjacent dimensional layers, capturing gas compounds that sublimate from the boundary between normal space and whatever lies beyond it. The phase-shift extraction pulls thirty-five percent more usable gas from each cloud than conventional collection methods — compounds that other harvesters leave behind because their instruments can't confirm they exist. The cargo hold is the smallest in class, deliberately so; the shield generators and dimensional stabilizers claimed the space. The hull underneath is fragile enough that losing shield coverage in a gas cloud is a terminal event. Pilots accept this tradeoff because nothing else in production matches the Phase Collector's extraction rate.

items.name: Pike
items.description: Fast Crimson interceptor. Catches runners before they reach the jump point.
items.lore:
In the Crimson Fleet, cowardice isn't running from a fight — it's
letting someone else run from one. The Pike exists to ensure that
doesn't happen. Oversized engines on an armored frame give it speed
5 to catch anything that tries to disengage, and 13 points of effective
armor keep it intact through the return fire. The two autocannons won't
win a damage race against a dedicated brawler like the Cleaver, but that's
not the point — the Pike holds targets in place until heavier firepower
arrives. Crimson instructors call it "the leash." Pilots who ask what
happens if heavier firepower doesn't arrive get assigned extra leash duty.

items.name: Pithead
items.description: Outer Rim overbuilt mining platform. Fast for its size, cheap, strips belts bare.
items.lore:
The Pithead is the only T4 mining platform with speed 2 — the
overclocked engines are technically out of spec, but they work, and
the Rim doesn't believe in specs anyway. Eighteen hundred cargo capacity
means it strips belts bare before slower competitors finish their
first load. At 85,000 credits, it's the cheapest T4 miner available
because the Rim builds ships from whatever's available rather than
whatever's optimal. The single weapon mount exists because frontier
mining operations attract attention, and the Rim's response to
attention is always armed.

items.name: Plausible Deniability
items.description: Outer Rim fleet command ship. Coordinates chaos at an institutional level.
items.lore:
When the Outer Rim needs to project actual military force — as opposed
to its usual approach of "several fast ships doing whatever they feel
like" — the Plausible Deniability-class coordinates the effort. Its
massive sensor and communications arrays can track and direct an entire
Rim battle group. The name reflects the ship's secondary purpose:
providing the Rim's civilian government with a credible claim that
whatever just happened was "unauthorized freelance activity" and not
a coordinated military operation.

items.name: Plenum
items.description: Voidborn dimensional fuel tanker. Holds more inside than out.
items.lore: In Voidborn cosmology the plenum is the conjectural substrate that fills what naive observers call empty space. The Plenum-class tanker takes the metaphor as a working specification: where lesser vessels carry fuel in tanks, the Plenum suspends it in folded volumes whose internal capacity exceeds the hull they are bolted to. Solarian docking equipment will not register a Plenum's load until a separate Voidborn calibration program is run, and on three documented occasions the Federation has billed a Plenum captain for fuel that did not appear on the receipt. Each captain accepted the charge without correction. The hull's adaptive shield envelope absorbs the structural strain of motion through compressed dimensional space, and the cargo manifest reads as a single field that is also twenty-four discrete reservoirs, depending on which observer is asked. There is no record of a Plenum needing the gun mount it does not have.

items.name: Polearm
items.description: Crimson deep-strike raider. Goes in armed, comes back loaded.
items.lore: Three weapon mounts on an exploration hull. The Polearm is the Fleet's wormhole probe — the first ship through, armed to handle whatever's waiting on the other side. Pirates, hostile territory, unknown systems with no refueling for dozens of jumps — the Polearm carries enough firepower to fight through all of it. Nearly every joule of fitting capacity goes to weapons and the anomaly detection array, leaving almost nothing for scientific instruments. Crimson Fleet command isn't interested in studying wormholes. They're interested in what's through them.

items.name: Polymath
items.description: Solarian grand-mastery commission — one hull that mines, fights, hauls, and surveys. None of it best in class, all of it competent, and built from a piece of every ship in the fleet.
items.lore:
The Confederacy does not, as a rule, build a ship to do everything — its design
committees prefer a specialist for each task, each with its own documentation.
The Polymath is the exception they grant exactly once, to a captain who has
mastered a discipline outright. It carries mining lasers, weapon mounts, survey
gear, and cargo holds in the same hull, and a review board will tell you,
accurately, that a dedicated miner pulls more ore, a cruiser brings more guns, a
hauler moves more freight, and an explorer sees farther. The Polymath's answer is
that it does all four without docking to refit, which no specialist can claim. It
is assembled from a component of nearly every vessel in the Solarian catalog, and
it is priced as though you bought one of each — because, in materials, you very
nearly did.
items.prestige_lock: Locked: prestige hull reserved for pilots who have earned a secret achievement.

items.name: Portcullis
items.description: Capital-grade Crimson interdictor. Traps entire fleets in normal space. Nobody runs.
items.lore:
The Bastille stops frigates from running. The Portcullis stops
fleets. Capital-grade warp disruption generators create a field
large enough to prevent every ship in a system from engaging jump
drives. The Portcullis is the highest-priority target in any
engagement — and the Crimson Fleet builds it knowing that. Four
defense slots and the thickest shields on any Crimson support
vessel keep it functional while absorbing the concentrated fire
of enemies desperate to escape. Crimson doctrine never deploys a
Portcullis without enough firepower to hold the cage closed.
Enemies trapped by a Portcullis have two options: surrender or
demonstrate why the Crimson Fleet brought a Devastator too.

items.name: Portfolio
items.description: Nebula multi-role vessel. Diversified capabilities for diversified income.
items.lore: "Never put all your credits in one venture." The Portfolio embodies the Federation's risk-management philosophy — a hull that can haul, fight, or run as market conditions demand. The default loadout covers all three: a weapon for pirates, a shield for survival, and a cargo expander for margins. Two weapon mounts and decent speed make it the only Nebula freighter that doesn't need an escort on contested routes. The Federation's marketing department calls it "diversified capability." Independent pilots call it the ship that does everything well enough and nothing perfectly.

items.name: Postulate
items.description: Solarian drone carrier. Deploys autonomous units from a well-documented command platform.
items.lore:
The Postulate-class takes a position and then proves it with drones. Solarian
drone doctrine requires each autonomous unit to file a mission report upon
return, and the Postulate's processing core dutifully catalogues them all.
The four utility slots support a variety of drone management and electronic
warfare configurations. Each drone's behavioral parameters are individually
peer-reviewed before deployment authorization.

items.name: Praecursor
items.description: Solarian pathfinder cruiser. Built to chart the deep unknown and survive the trip back.
items.lore: Solarian pathfinder doctrine measures success in margins: percent of fuel reserve unspent on arrival, percent of bearings within drift tolerance, percent of refined fuel that hits the tank rather than venting to vacuum. The Praecursor is the hull built to those margins. The pathfinder drive plots galactic bearings with confidence intervals attached to every heading; the integrated gas harvester feeds a hydrogen burner that drips fuel directly into the tank; the eleven-hundred-unit reserve is sized so that even a wasted refining stage still gets a careful pilot home. Pathfinder Corps certification on a Praecursor takes four years of simulator hours and a real-coordinates qualifying drift the Corps does not publish details of. The Bureau of Deep Survey reports the casualty rate annually and considers any year under three percent a success.

items.name: Prayer
items.description: Cargo containers welded to an engine. Pilot straps in outside. No shields, no weapons, no excuses.
items.lore:
The Prayer-class is not a ship. It is cargo containers welded to an
engine with a seat bolted to the outside. There is no cockpit. There
is no life support. There is no shield generator, no weapon mount, no
defense system, and no module slot of any kind. The pilot wears a
spacesuit and holds on. Five hundred and forty units of cargo capacity at tier
one — more than most ships three tiers higher. The catch is everything
else: 40 hull means a stiff breeze is lethal, and there is literally
nothing you can do to improve the ship's survivability. It cannot be
upgraded. It cannot be armed. It can only carry things from one place
to another and hope nothing goes wrong along the way. Named for what
the pilot does before undocking.

items.name: Precept
items.description: Solarian patrol craft. Scanner-heavy law enforcement and inspection vessel.
items.lore:
A precept is a rule or principle governing personal conduct — and the
Precept-class exists to ensure those rules are followed. The Confederacy's
patrol vessel carries more sensor equipment than weapons, because the
Solarian philosophy of law enforcement prioritizes detection over
deterrence. The onboard scanning suite can identify cargo manifests,
registration anomalies, and outstanding warrants at distances that make
evasion impractical. One weapon mount provides "persuasive capability"
for non-compliant vessels. The official hail begins: "This is a routine
inspection. Please transmit your documentation."

items.name: Premiere
items.description: Nebula grand liner. The most luxurious vessel in the Federation fleet catalog.
items.lore:
The Premiere-class is the Federation's flagship civilian vessel — a
floating embassy for commerce, diplomacy, and the demonstration of
wealth. Gold-trimmed interiors, panoramic observation decks, and
shields rated for capital-ship engagement ensure passengers travel
in both comfort and safety. The Federation books the Premiere for
treaty negotiations, because nothing says "negotiate from strength"
like hosting talks on a ship worth more than your opponent's fleet.

items.name: Principia
items.description: Solarian research shuttle. Extra CPU for scientific instruments.
items.lore:
The Principia carries more processing power than most ships twice its size
— the Confederacy's standard loadout for orbital survey work requires it.
No weapons by design; the sensor array and three utility hardpoints consume
the engineering budget. Defensive modules can be fitted for work near contested
borders, though the requisition forms require three levels of approval. Named
after Newton's treatise, because the Confederacy names everything after treatises.

items.name: Probable Cause
items.description: Outer Rim blockade runner. When subtlety fails, speed succeeds.
items.lore: Speed 5 on a medium hull. The Probable Cause represents the Outer Rim's finest tradition of solving every problem by going faster. Named by a pilot who pointed out that "existing near a Probable Cause is itself probable cause for a customs inspection," these ships run blockades, deliver contraband, carry diplomatic pouches, and generally make border authorities very unhappy. The fuel reserves support indirect routes through systems nobody patrols because nobody expected anyone to go there.

items.name: Promenade
items.description: Solarian liner. Diplomatic transport with academic conference facilities.
items.lore: The Promenade-class is the Confederacy's idea of luxury travel: comfortable cabins, excellent life support, and a fully equipped lecture hall. Passenger amenities include a research-grade library, three seminar rooms, and a lounge with panoramic viewports certified to withstand "all anticipated environmental conditions." Popular for inter-system academic conferences, faculty relocations, and the occasional diplomatic function where everyone pretends the after-dinner talk is optional.

items.name: Prospect
items.description: Nebula starter vessel. Pre-loaded price database. Best cargo in its class.
items.lore:
The Prospect comes with the Federation's compliments — and a pre-loaded
database of current commodity prices across 200 stations, a loyalty chip
tied to your Federation trade account, and a glossy brochure outlining
upgrade paths starting at just 1,999 credits. The expanded cargo hold
isn't generosity; it's an investment in future transaction volume. The
fuel-efficient drive was a practical decision — every credit spent on fuel
is a credit not spent at a Federation marketplace. Includes a 90-day
trial of Federation Premium Trade Intelligence (auto-renews at
competitive rates).

items.name: Prospectus
items.description: Nebula speed scout. Fastest exploration hull in production — gets there first, sets the terms.
items.lore: Whoever maps the route sets the terms. The Prospectus reaches uncharted systems while other scouts are still calculating jump sequences — the fastest exploration hull in production, built to cover more ground per hour than anything else flying a survey flag. The fuel tank is oversized to compensate for what speed costs: at this velocity, range is a resource that burns fast, and smart captains plan refueling stops rather than assuming they can reach the edge and come back. Market-analysis sensors assess commercial potential in real time — resource deposits, traffic patterns, station demand gaps — so the data arrives formatted as a business case before the competition has even departed. The hull is thin and the weapon mount is an afterthought. Speed is the defense.

items.name: Qualia
items.description: Voidborn deep explorer. Cloaked, shielded, built to return from places others do not.
items.lore: Qualia — the subjective qualities of conscious experience. The Voidborn chose this name for their deep exploration vessel because it does not merely survey. It persists. Layered shields regenerate under fire, the cloaking system defeats targeting locks, and the scan-resistant hull reveals little to hostile scanners. The Qualia is built for lawless space where other scouts become wreckage — unarmed, because its survival strategy is not to fight but to simply not be where the weapons land. Pilots who fly the Qualia into dangerous space tend to come back. They also tend to come back quiet.

items.name: Quorum
items.description: Solarian cruiser. Balanced multi-role warship with committee-approved firepower.
items.lore: The Quorum-class cruiser was designed by consensus, which in the Confederacy means it took four years and three redesigns. The result is a ship that does everything well and nothing brilliantly — exactly as the seventeen-member design committee intended. The balanced loadout supports fleet roles from patrol to escort to independent operations. Every system has a backup, every backup has documentation, and every document has been reviewed by at least two committees.

items.name: Ransack
items.description: Armed Crimson freighter. Carries cargo or carries loot — same ship, different manifest.
items.lore: The Crimson Fleet doesn't build unarmed freighters. The concept offends them. The Ransack ships with twin autocannons and armor plating — a loadout that turns cargo runs into something closer to armed patrols. The cargo bay is generous by Crimson standards, which means it's modest by anyone else's. What the Ransack lacks in speed — the armor plate drops it to a crawl — it makes up for in the certainty that the cargo arrives intact. Fleet logistics classifies Ransack crews as either "merchants" or "acquisition specialists," depending on which direction the cargo is moving.

items.name: Rapid Smelter
items.description: Outer Rim fast smelting platform. High throughput, low finesse. Bolted together but it works.
items.lore:
The Rapid Smelter is the Rim's answer to refinery ships: fast, cheap,
and good enough. The smelting systems process basic ores into refined
materials at twice the speed of Solarian precision refineries, at half
the quality. The Rim considers this an acceptable trade-off — volume
beats quality when you're supplying frontier operations that need
materials yesterday. Speed 2 makes it mobile enough to follow mining
operations rather than waiting at a fixed location. The entire smelting
assembly was salvaged from three different decommissioned stations and
welded into a hull that the original engineers would not recognize.

items.name: Ravager
items.description: Crimson armored mining platform. Fortress hull, can fight back. The Fleet's heavy extraction asset.
items.lore:
The Ravager-class is what happens when the Crimson Fleet applies
capital ship engineering to asteroid mining. Twelve hundred points of
hull and fifty-five points of armor make it nearly indestructible by
anything short of a dedicated assault force. Two weapon mounts keep
contested mining fields clear while five utility slots drive
industrial-scale extraction — the Fleet maintains a firm distinction
between the tools that mine and the tools that fight. Fourteen
hundred forty cargo capacity fills over sustained extraction operations
that other empires would call a siege. The Ravager doesn't mine a
system — it claims it.

items.name: Reaver
items.description: Crimson gas hauler. High-pressure containment compresses collected gas to half volume. Armed, because of course it is.
items.lore: The Reaver-class is more cargo hauler than gas harvester, and it is not subtle about it. The largest effective gas hold in its class means a single Reaver can strip a cloud in one pass and haul the take home without a support ship. The reinforced hull and default armor plating add mass — the Reaver is the slowest vessel in the Crimson Fleet by a comfortable margin. Pilots who want speed can pull the plate, but most keep it. A Reaver parks in a nebula, fills its hold, and leaves. The weapon mount ensures that anyone who objects to the parking job regrets the interruption.

items.name: Receivership
items.description: Nebula heavy salvage platform. Recovers entire battlefields' worth of assets in a single operation.
items.lore: The Receivership-class carries the largest cargo bay fitted to any salvager in production and a proprietary asset-tracking system that assigns serial numbers to individual hull fragments before they reach the hold. A single Receivership can strip a medium engagement site in one pass — armor plating, electronics, structural members, all catalogued and sorted for resale before the drive cooldown completes. Insurance underwriters across the sector have designated it a preferred recovery platform, which reduces premiums enough that the Federation's marketing division built an entire campaign around it. The hull plating is decorative at best. If someone is shooting at the Receivership, the operation has already failed the risk assessment.

items.name: Reckoning
items.description: Crimson assault titan. Takes stations by force. The Fleet's ultimate boarding platform.
items.lore: A ship designed to physically dock with enemy stations and deliver a small army through breaching systems that can cut through anything short of neutronium. The armor is built to absorb sustained point-blank fire from fixed emplacements while eight weapon mounts suppress station defenses during approach. The boarding capacity can seize and hold a medium-sized station in a single operation. Building a Reckoning is a statement of intent — the Crimson Fleet doesn't build one unless it plans to take something worth taking. And the Crimson Fleet always plans to take something worth taking.

items.name: Reclaim
items.description: Nebula fast-response salvager. Afterburner-equipped to reach wreck sites before the competition.
items.lore: Federation salvage contracts have a clause most operators skip past: first on-site gets priority recovery rights. The Reclaim was redesigned around that clause. An afterburner and upgraded engines make it the fastest salvager in its class — an unusual design choice for the Federation, which normally optimizes for margin over mobility. The tradeoff is fuel: at full burn, the Reclaim drinks its tank dry in a dozen jumps, and smart operators learn which wrecks are worth the sprint and which aren't. The weapon mount was dropped to free up fitting capacity, leaving the most flexible utility bay in its class. Federation salvage crews don't fight over wrecks — they outrun the competition and file the paperwork first.

items.name: Recursion
items.description: Voidborn aggressive interceptor. Faster and more heavily armed than any other Collective combat ship.
items.lore: The Collective built the Recursion to answer a question the other empires didn't think to ask: what happens when a Voidborn ship stops being patient? The additional weapon mount and faster hull make it the most aggressive platform the Collective has fielded — still shielded, still regenerating, but closing distance and pressing attacks instead of waiting for them. Pilots describe combat in the Recursion as "being on the other side of the conversation for once." The name refers to the engagement loop: approach, fire, regenerate, approach again. Each pass refines the targeting solution. The enemy's defenses do not receive the same iterative improvement.

items.name: Red Herring
items.description: A recovered Crimson Stiletto, repatched and repurposed. The targeting protocols are gone. The sensor suite has been jury-rigged with salvaged arrays that do one job: identify what a ship is carrying and how hard it will fight back. The rest is original — meaning it's still fast, which is the only thing that mattered.
items.lore: Every pirate scout wing has a few of these. The Crimson Fleet builds the Stiletto to be fast and hard to catch — pirates agree completely on both points, which is why they steal them whenever possible. Stripped of Crimson targeting protocols and refitted with salvaged sensor arrays, the Red Herring does one thing the original never did: it tells you exactly what a freighter is carrying before the raiding squad commits. The name comes from what happens next. By the time the freighter captain realizes they were scanned, the ship is already gone — and something much worse is on the way.

items.name: Reliquary
items.description: Solarian fleet carrier for the captain who owns everything — the largest ship bay ever certified, sized to move an entire collection between ports. Lightly armed; what it guards is the cargo, and the cargo is your fleet.
items.lore:
To own one of every ship class is, by the Confederacy's reckoning, less an
achievement than a logistics problem: a fleet that large cannot fly itself home,
and no existing carrier could move more than a fraction of it. The Reliquary was
commissioned to close that gap. Its bay is the largest ever certified for a mobile
hull — a cathedral of docking cradles, gantries, and umbilicals, each rated to
hold and service a different class, so the collection travels together rather than
scattered across a dozen stations. It mounts only enough weaponry to discourage
the opportunist, because the Reliquary is not built to fight; it is built to arrive
with everything you have ever owned still aboard. The Fleet Logistics Review,
which once filed a minority dissent recommending a ten-bay Convoy, is understood
to consider the matter finally settled.
items.prestige_lock: Locked: prestige hull reserved for pilots who have earned the "Shipwright Supreme" achievement.

items.name: Remedy
items.description: Solarian repair ship. Mobile maintenance platform with diagnostic precision.
items.lore: The Remedy-class diagnoses ship malfunctions the way a Solarian physician diagnoses patients: exhaustively, with multiple independent verification methods, and with a written report afterward. Five utility slots accommodate repair drones, welding arrays, and material fabrication systems. The diagnostic CPU identifies structural failures down to the molecular level. Field-repaired vessels are issued a "Certificate of Provisional Airworthiness" that somehow manages to be both reassuring and ominous.

items.name: Repo
items.description: A Nebula Reclaim stripped of Federation livery and quarterly performance metrics. The cargo bays are intact. The tow system is intact. The part where it files recovery reports with investors has been removed.
items.lore: Pirates keep making wrecks, and the materials don't haul themselves. The Repo is a stolen Reclaim with the Federation's processing arrays ripped out and the cargo bays expanded — the biggest hold of any salvager in its class. The tow system and extended fuel range that made the original worth stealing are intact. The real-time asset valuation software is gone — salvage components don't replicate Nebula electronics, and pirates don't need a ship to tell them what a wreck is worth. They already know. They made it.

items.name: Repo Man
items.description: Outer Rim speed miner. Fastest mining vessel in its class. Gets in, grabs ore, gets out.
items.lore: Fastest mining vessel in its class, built from racing hull components that the Patchwork repurposed with cheerful disregard for manufacturer warranties. The hold is small — the engines took the space that cargo wanted — but compression storage and quick turnaround times mean more runs per shift than any other miner in the field. Repo Man pilots treat mining like a smash-and-grab: laser on, fill what you can, engines hot before anyone with guns shows up. The autocannon is there for the days when the engines aren't quite hot enough.

items.name: Reserve
items.description: Nebula fuel tanker. Keeps the fleet moving and the credits flowing.
items.lore: The Reserve-class keeps Federation convoys operational on routes that would strand lighter ships. Massive internal fuel bunkerage and pressurized cargo holds for fuel resale make the Reserve both a logistical asset and a profit center. The Federation's fuel pricing at deep-space waypoints is described internally as "competitive" and externally as "the only option for 50 lightyears."

items.name: Residuum
items.description: Voidborn ghost salvager. Cloaked approach, shield-tanked hull, and the tow capacity to drag wreckage away before anyone notices.
items.lore: The Residuum-class arrives at debris fields the way Voidborn do most things — without announcing itself. The integrated cloaking system and scan-resistant hull mean the Residuum is already sorting wreckage by the time competing salvagers detect the field. What it lacks in cargo volume it compensates for with the strongest towing rig in its weight class and shields thick enough to keep working under fire. Filament-thin tendrils extend into the debris, anchoring to hull fragments with a grip strength that startles engineers who inspect the moorings afterward. Pilots report the ship runs warmer during towing operations, as though the effort is metabolic. By the time anyone else arrives, the Residuum has dragged the best pieces somewhere difficult to find.

items.name: Resonance Miner
items.description: Voidborn adaptive mining platform. Massive fitting capacity, minimal defaults, endless possibility.
items.lore: Asteroids subjected to Resonance-class operations develop geometric voids in their remaining structure — perfect polyhedra carved from natural rock by a mining laser that appears to understand crystallographic planes no geological survey has documented. The ship's fitting capacity is enormous for its class, most of it deliberately left empty — the single mining laser and shield booster are a starting point, not a finished design. The shield array regenerates fast enough that most environmental hazards resolve themselves. The hull underneath, at minimal armor, conspicuously does not. Pilots who treat the Resonance Miner as fragile are correct. Pilots who treat it as inflexible are not.

items.name: Reticence
items.description: Voidborn executive transport. Privacy as a service.
items.lore:
The Collective observed that other empires' executives advertise their
movements with gold trim and escort fighters, then pay separately to be
protected from the attention. The Reticence resolves the contradiction
by being unremarkable in every measurable spectrum. Four cabins in full
acoustic isolation. The manifest is encrypted, the itinerary is a
rumor, and the viewports display a route the ship may or may not have
taken. Clients debark rested and unbothered, which is the entire
product. The Collective does not advertise the Reticence. Its clients
appreciate that too.

items.name: Revenue
items.description: Nebula yield-optimized gas harvester. Maximum return per trip through superior extraction efficiency.
items.lore: Federation actuaries redesigned the gas harvesting model around return per trip rather than range, and the numbers were compelling: best-in-class yield bonus, compression-rated cargo bays, and a shorter fuel tank that forces tighter route planning. Longer routes mean more fuel burned, more exposure, more risk per credit earned. The Revenue makes shorter trips and better margins. The quarterly earnings reports from Revenue-class operations are the most consistent in the Federation's industrial portfolio, which is exactly the kind of sentence that gets a Nebula procurement officer promoted.

items.name: Rift Siphon
items.description: Voidborn gas extraction capital. Opens dimensional rifts to harvest exotic gases from parallel realities.
items.lore:
The Rift Siphon-class opens stable micro-rifts to parallel dimensions
and siphons exotic gases that don't exist in normal space. The
collection membranes extend into dimensional fractures that the ship
itself generates, capturing compounds with properties that violate
every known law of chemistry. Twenty-two hundred shield points
maintain the dimensional barriers that keep the rifts stable — an
unshielded rift collapse is described in Collective safety manuals as
"geometrically catastrophic." The gases harvested by the Rift Siphon
are unique to Voidborn space and cannot be obtained by any other
means. What the Collective does with these exotic gases is classified
at the highest level of Collective security. The ship's existence is
not classified. What it produces is.

items.name: Rime
items.description: Voidborn ice phaser. Shield-dominant platform with phase-shifted extraction that compresses harvested ice to half volume.
items.lore: The Rime-class does not mine ice. It convinces ice to relocate. The Collective's cryo-extraction system uses localized phase-shifting to separate ice from its parent body at the molecular level, producing samples of extraordinary purity. Pilots report that the ship's interior temperature drops during extraction — by exactly the amount the extracted ice's temperature rises. Voidborn engineers call this "thermal sympathy." Everyone else calls it "deeply unsettling." The shield envelope that protects the Rime during operations is significantly overspecified for an industrial vessel, with regeneration fast enough to shrug off most opportunistic attacks. The open utility architecture accepts additional modules without complaint, a flexibility that Voidborn engineers describe as "the ship adapting to its pilot's needs." Whether the adaptation is mutual remains an open question.

items.name: Rock Eater
items.description: Outer Rim deep-range mining cruiser. Fuel-efficient drive mines fields nobody else can reach.
items.lore: Rim miners work fields that other empires don't bother charting — three sectors from the nearest station, past the patrol routes, where the rocks are rich because nobody else makes the trip. The Rock Eater was built for that run. The fuel-efficient drive stretches a massive tank across forty-four jumps of operational range at speed 2, and the dual mining lasers ensure the trip was worth making. The hull won't win any toughness awards and the fitting budget is tight, but the Rock Eater reaches deposits that no other miner can. Cheapest T3 miner on the market. Rim philosophy: spend credits on fuel, not on the ship.

items.name: Runner
items.description: A faction speed-runner — stripped to the engine and tuned to cross the map at the hard speed limit while barely sipping fuel. Small hold, no guns. It exists to get there first.
items.lore:
The Runner is the cartel's answer to a closing window. It travels at the hard
limit the galaxy imposes — every jump resolves in the shortest span physics
allows — and a tuned, frugal drive lets it hold that pace clear across the map
without stopping to refuel. The hold is small and there is nothing to fight with,
because neither is the job: the job is to be the first ship to arrive while the
deal is still good. A faction that runs Runners is a faction that has noticed
money moves faster than cargo, and decided to keep up.
items.prestige_lock: Locked: prestige hull reserved for members of a faction that has earned the "Blitz Economy" achievement.

items.name: Running Tab
items.description: Hell's Bells with condensed dark matter and flex polymer stripped out. Speed 4 at scale three, rebuilt from steel and salvage. The Outer Rim engineers would not recognize it as their work. The speed they would recognize.
items.lore:
The Outer Rim built the Hell's Bells by answering one question seventeen times in a row: what if there were more engines? The result was a cruiser that looks, from most angles, like an engine cluster that grew a cockpit by accident — thruster nacelles stacked and angled in directions that no single engineering philosophy would sanction, held in alignment by flex polymer and the structural magic of materials that cost more than most ships weigh. Fast. Suspiciously fast. The kind of fast where you check your instruments because your instruments must be wrong.
Pirates stripped the dark matter cores and the flex polymer. They replaced the missing mass budget with additional conventional thruster housings — more of them, uglier, bolted wherever the clearance allowed, exhausting across each other in ways that technically shouldn't work. The Running Tab is louder than a Hell's Bells, its exhaust signature is visible across three sectors, and it is faster than the ship it came from because it turns out the Outer Rim's real engineering insight was not the exotic materials. It was: more thrust, less weight, argue with the results later.
The name comes from what it leaves behind. Every system it passes through has a running tab of damage, encounters, sensor ghosts, and unanswered questions. The ship is always somewhere else before the accounting starts.

items.name: Scrutiny
items.description: Solarian customs interceptor. More scanner than ship. The Confederacy considers this an acceptable ratio.
items.lore:
The Scrutiny-class carries scanning equipment that would be classified
as surveillance hardware in any other context. The Confederacy classifies
it as "routine inspection capability" and declines to elaborate on the
distinction. Three utility slots accommodate the full sensor suite:
spectral analysis, cargo density mapping, and a signature library that
is updated daily from Confederacy central records. One weapon mount is
included for "procedural compliance enforcement." The official customs
hail is seventeen words long and includes a citation number.

items.name: Severance Package
items.description: Imperator Dross's flagship. A Crimson Guillotine rebuilt without the fury alloy and siege plating that gave the original its armor — the rebuilt hull takes hits harder. The cargo bays and tow system are untouched. The Crimson ship followed battle groups and processed what remained. This one follows Dross. The distinction between "battle group" and "Dross" is largely semantic at this point.
items.lore:
The Crimson Fleet built the Guillotine because reducing wreck fields to raw materials is skilled work that deserves a dedicated platform. The runner-up name was "Carrion." The fury alloy and siege plating are gone — the rebuilt hull runs on steel and salvage, takes hits harder, and has the same cargo capacity, the same tow system, and the same four weapon mounts. The only thing that changed is whose battle group it follows.
The Crimson version followed at a respectful distance. Dross's version leads.
The Dross Citadel station is built from the wreckage of three different warships. Most of the construction material came through this ship's cargo bays. Dross has been operating on the main inter-empire routes long enough that the station's architectural history is visible in the hull panels — different ship classes, different alloys, different failure modes. The Severance Package doesn't distinguish between categories. Everything eventually becomes cargo.

items.name: Shard
items.description: Crimson starter vessel. Repurposed combat drone. Mines with the utility slot, fights with the weapon slots.
items.lore:
The Shard was never designed as a mining vessel. It was a combat drone —
autonomous, disposable, built to absorb fire while delivering ordnance.
When the Crimson Fleet needed a starter ship, their engineers did what
Crimson engineers always do: they added a mining laser to the utility
hardpoint and called it done. The weapon slots are original equipment,
untouched. The armor plating no one bothered to remove is a bonus. Crimson
pilots wouldn't have it any other way — a ship that mines and fights
simultaneously isn't a compromise, it's a statement of values.

items.name: Siege Breaker
items.description: Crimson yield-optimized mining cruiser. Extracts more ore per cycle than anything else in the field.
items.lore: Fleet engineers spent three design cycles trying to build a better mining laser before realizing the extraction system wasn't the bottleneck — the targeting was. The Siege Breaker's dual lasers operate on a synchronized firing pattern that hits the same fracture point from two angles, pulling thirty-five percent more usable ore from each rock than sequential extraction. The cargo hold is smaller than competing designs because the engineering committee refused to sacrifice hull integrity for storage. Crimson mining doctrine: bring home less per trip, but bring home more per rock, and make sure the ship comes home at all.

items.name: Siege Drill
items.description: Crimson artillery mining platform. Dual railguns keep the field clear while the laser works.
items.lore: Fleet doctrine classifies asteroid fields as territory, and territory requires fire superiority. The Siege Drill mounts dual railguns alongside its mining laser — slow-firing electromagnetic accelerators that resolve claim disputes at range, before the other party closes to where things get complicated. The mining laser works the asteroid while the railguns discourage approach from any direction. Fleet engineers used every available CPU cycle fitting the loadout, which means the ship does exactly what it was designed for and nothing else. Nobody buys a Siege Drill for the cargo capacity.

items.name: Silent Tide
items.description: Voidborn stealth carrier. Moves your fleet without anyone knowing the fleet moved.
items.lore: The Voidborn do not announce fleet movements. They consider the announcement itself a tactical failure. The Silent Tide-class carries six ships with an integrated cloaking field strong enough to mask the whole formation — hull signatures, engine wash, navigational emissions. The Collective reviewed three operations compromised not by Voidborn vessels, but by the emission trails of their escorts. Their conclusion was that the problem was having escorts at all. The Silent Tide resolves this by becoming the escort, the carrier, and the point of first contact simultaneously — a single hull where there was previously a formation, carrying inside it the formation that was never there. What is not there cannot be detected.

items.name: Smelter
items.description: Nebula mobile refinery. Converts raw ore to finished materials in the field.
items.lore:
The Smelter-class eliminates the most expensive part of the mining
supply chain: hauling raw ore back to a station for processing. Onboard
smelting furnaces, chemical separators, and automated quality assurance
systems convert raw materials into market-ready commodities in the
field. The Federation calculates that a Smelter increases mining fleet
profitability by 60% by cutting transport costs and time-to-market.

items.name: Solarian Foundation
items.description: Solarian budget explorer. Fuel-efficient drive stretches a modest tank into real survey range.
items.lore: The Confederacy needed survey platforms faster than the premium production line could deliver, so it designed one from common stock materials with an assembly time that undercuts everything else in the exploration class. Lower CPU means sensors run sequentially rather than in parallel; three utility bays mean the pilot selects which systems matter most. Both were acceptable compromises. Fuel range was not — the engineering team classified it non-negotiable in the first design review, then solved it through drive optimization rather than a larger tank. The result burns less fuel per jump than any other exploration hull at its speed, stretching a modest tank into working survey range. Unarmed by design: the Foundation's mandate is coverage, not engagement.

items.name: Solipsism
items.description: Voidborn ghost. A hull built to go everywhere unseen and do nothing but watch.
items.lore:
The Solipsism is the perfect observer. It goes anywhere — through
blockades, past picket lines, into systems whose owners would object
strenuously if they knew it had arrived — and it is seen by nothing.
The cloaking envelope and the sensor-scattering hull together render
it absent from every instrument trained on the space it occupies. What
it brings back is everything it saw and nothing else. It carries no
weapons, because a weapon implies an intention to be noticed, and being
noticed is the only way a Solipsism dies. The Collective regards an
engagement as a failure of the design rather than a test of it. The
hull is fragile, slow to no purpose it would ever pursue, and incapable
of carrying anything worth taking; it pays a great deal to be a ghost
that does one thing. It watches, and it returns, and it tells you what
is there.

items.name: Spit and Prayer
items.description: Outer Rim deep-range gas harvester. Big fuel tank, afterburner, reaches clouds nobody else can.
items.lore: An oversized fuel tank lets the Spit and Prayer reach gas clouds in dead-end systems that other harvesters can't round-trip to. The default afterburner is there for when the neighborhood gets unfriendly — Rim pilots treat it like a reserve parachute: comforting to have, expensive to use. The hold is small for a T2 harvester, and compression storage only goes so far — that's the price of an engine bay built for escape velocity. You don't send a Spit and Prayer to fill a station. You send it to find the cloud nobody else can reach, and it comes back with just enough to make the trip worth arguing about.

items.name: Standing Order
items.description: Sovereign Crix's flagship. A Crimson Overlord without the drone command module, sensor cluster, and Crimson siege plating that defined the original. The command suite is intact. The fleet coordination systems are intact. The weapon mounts are intact. Crix is the only pirate warlord in the sector who actually uses all of these as designed.
